title: Assess the setting before proposing the service
focus: Schools, nurseries, healthcare settings and workplace canteens have different users, facilities and approval requirements. Start with a detailed operational brief rather than an event menu. Define meal volumes, service days, dietary needs and the documentation your organisation requires. The proposed culinary partner and site arrangements must be assessed against that brief before any commitment. A clear specification gives procurement and operations a shared basis for reviewing suitability, responsibilities and the commercial proposal.

sections.title: Build a repeatable service specification
paragraphs: An ongoing food-service arrangement needs a more detailed brief than a one-off event. Define the number of meals, service days, delivery or preparation location and the people responsible for receiving and approving the food. If volumes vary, explain how changes will be communicated and confirmed.

Menu cycles, portions, dietary requirements and reporting should be discussed with the proposed provider. The relevant organisation may have its own approval process and documentation requirements, which need to be understood before a service is agreed. Avoid assuming that an event menu automatically suits a recurring institutional setting.

A useful proposal sets out the responsibilities on both sides, including facilities, equipment, service windows and review points. Any specialist requirements should be assessed explicitly. The result should be a workable specification that the organisation and culinary partner can evaluate together before moving into delivery.

sections.title: Give every guest a considered option
paragraphs: Collect dietary requirements before the final menu is agreed. Record how many guests each requirement applies to and distinguish preferences from allergies or other essential restrictions. A clear list helps the culinary team assess suitable dishes and the preparation arrangements they would need.

A vegetarian or vegan choice should feel like a complete part of the menu. Consider its portion, accompaniments and presentation alongside the other dishes, rather than removing an ingredient and assuming the result will be satisfying. Sauces, garnishes, breads and desserts also need attention.

Allergy requests require a specific discussion of ingredients and kitchen conditions. Labels and separate serving utensils can support a plan, but they do not by themselves guarantee the absence of cross-contact. Share the details early so the team can assess the request honestly and confirm what can be accommodated before you book.

sections.title: Compare the complete proposal
paragraphs: Read the price together with the menu and service scope. Two proposals can have different totals because one includes equipment, staffing or a longer service period that the other does not. Compare them against the same guest count and requirements before deciding which is the better fit.

Check the minimum order, included hours, delivery or transport arrangements and how applicable VAT is shown. If the menu uses a starting price, ask which choices could change it. Premium ingredients, additional stations, extended service and extra hospitality support may need separate pricing.

The written proposal should also explain the payment schedule and the terms for changes or cancellation. Use the terms attached to your booking, as a private occasion and a corporate contract may have different arrangements. A clear comparison gives you confidence in the decision and helps avoid assumptions about what a headline price includes.

sections.title: Finish with a clear handover and collection plan
paragraphs: Good catering continues through the end of service. Confirm which areas the team will clear, what happens to hired equipment and who will receive any final handover. A venue may need the space returned by a particular time, while a private home may have specific instructions for access after guests leave.

Discuss leftover food with the team rather than assuming everything can be packed and kept in the same way. Any handover should follow the instructions appropriate to the food and conditions involved. If you want containers or another arrangement, raise that before the event so it can be assessed.

For repeat bookings, note what worked well and what you would change. Useful feedback on portions, menu choices and service timing gives the next proposal a stronger starting point. A clear finish leaves you with fewer loose ends and helps make the next occasion easier to organise.
